newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: LIBERALS ASKED TO CHOSE NEW DIRECTOR NEXT WEEK
The Federal Liberal Party President, Tony Staley, is calling an urgent tele-conference of the party's executive next week to decide on a replacement for Federal Director, Andrew Robb.
Mr Robb is leaving after nine and a half years with the Party, seven of those as Federal Director.
He's widely credited with playing a crucial role in the Liberal's Federal election victory last year.
Tony Staley says the resignation wasn't a shock, but people did try to persude Mr Robb to stay on.
Mr Staley says it's undertandable that Mr Robb wants to make another career while he's still young.
ACTU SAYS CHILDCARE CUTS WILL LEAD TO CLOSURES
A-C-T-U President Jenni George says many community childcare centres will close if cuts of 400 million dollars in Government funding go ahead.
Ms George says under the cuts, proposed in a leaked budget document, childcare costs would rise 20-dollars a week per child.
She says the leaking of the document is a cynical exercise designed to keep women out of the workforce.
Ms George says women are already having to drop out of work because childcare costs too much.
She adds there's nothing family-friendly about a government which provides small relief through a family tax initiative then argues for a measly eight dollar wage increase.
HOWARD STICKS TO PLAN TO RESTRICT NATIVE TITLE ON LEASES
The Prime Minister is not budging on his plan to restrict native title rights on pastoral leases, despite criticism from indigenous leaders and the National Party.
The plan stops short of full extinguishment of native title rights but downgrades Aborigines' access to the land.

Mr Howard's told ABC Radio his plan does not restrict native title but does deliver security and makes the Native Title Act Mr Howard is meeting Aboriginal negotiators and Queensland Premier Rob Borbidge today, ahead of putting his plan to Premiers and Federal Cabinet on Monday.
Indigenous leaders say the proposal is not fair, with some saying the Prime Minister's not willing to discuss the fundamental Aboriginal right to negotiate resource development and land use.
HOWARD SIGNALS END TO CROSS-MEDIA OWNERSHIP RULES
The Prime Minister says a media company needs a strong domestic base if it's to be a flag-waver for Australia around the world.

In the strongest signal yet that the Government will scrap the existing cross-media ownership rules, Mr Howard said they inspired by the former Labor Government's malice against the Fairfax newspaper group.
Mr Howard has this week had talks with media proprieters including Kerry Packer, who's keen to acquire Fairfax, but at present may not control both television and print outlets in the same city.
Mr Howard has told ABC Radio the idea of cross-media prohibitions is ridiculous, and several factors including the challenge of the Internet to classified advertising have to be taken into account.
Meanwhile Victorian Premier Jeff Kennett says he would prefer to have Australians own our media outlets rather than foreigners, even if it contradicts cross-media ownership laws.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
